The authors have calculated the time-dependent, nonequilibrium thermal and ionization history of gas cooling radiatively from 10^6 K in a one-dimensional, planar, steady-state flow model of the galactic fountain.
The initial flow velocity is v_0 ~ 100 km/s, comparable to the sound speed of a 10^6 K gas.
The initial density is n_H,0 ~ 2x10^-2 cm^-3, in reasonable agreement with other observational estimates.
The size of the cooling region is D ~ 40 pc.

The authors' new calculations, which take full account of radiative transfer, confirm the importance of self-ionization in enabling the flow to match observed galactic halo column densities of C IV, Si IV, and N V, as well as UV emission from C IV and O III].
The new calculations allow for a much larger range of cooling region sizes (D ≤ 0.15 pc) compared to previous optically thin calculations.

The cooling process reaches a 'plateau' stage at around 10^4 K, where the cooling time becomes much longer than the sound crossing time, and the pressure in this stage remains fixed at the value of the internal pressure of the cooling region at the end of the isochoric, rapid cooling phase.
The authors also compare predicted Hα fluxes, UV line emission, and broadband X-ray fluxes with observed values.
One-dimensional numerical hydrodynamical calculations including the effects of radiative cooling are also presented in the paper.

The model's ability to match observed galactic halo column densities and UV/X-ray emission suggests that self-ionization plays an important role in the thermal and ionization history of the gas in the galactic fountain.
The paper investigates the time-dependent, non-equilibrium thermal and ionization history of gas cooling radiatively from 10^6 K.
The authors use a one-dimensional, planar, steady-state flow model of the galactic fountain.
The effects of radiative transfer and self-ionization are included in the calculations.
The model parameters include the initial flow velocity, initial density, and size of the cooling region.
The model is compared to observational data on column densities, UV line emission, and X-ray fluxes in the galactic halo.
